lines.text: Stone circles, pyramids, temples in the jungle and towers of steel. These are the wonders of the world, in the order people built them.
It begins on a hilltop in Turkey, where hunter-gatherers raised rings of carved stone pillars long before anyone farmed.
On Salisbury Plain in England, prehistoric people raised a ring of huge stones, lined up with the midsummer sunrise. Why, we still debate.
In Egypt, the Great Pyramid of Khufu rose at Giza, the tallest building on Earth for thousands of years, and the last ancient wonder still standing.
Beside it, a lion with a human face was carved from the living rock: the Great Sphinx, keeping watch over the desert.
Along the Indus, Mohenjo-daro was laid out with straight streets, brick houses and drains, a city planned with remarkable care.
At Thebes, the pharaohs began Karnak, a temple of giant columns that they would keep enlarging for some two thousand years.
Ramesses the Second had four colossal statues of himself cut into a cliff at Abu Simbel. In the 1960s the whole temple was moved, to save it from the Nile.
In China, states began building walls to guard their northern frontier. Over many dynasties they became the Great Wall.
Greek writers praised the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, terraces built for a king's wife. No Babylonian text mentions them, and they remain a mystery.
At Ephesus, a vast marble temple rose for the goddess Artemis, burned by an arsonist and rebuilt, until it was finally taken apart.
In the mountains of Iran, the Persian kings built Persepolis, where carved stairways show the peoples of the empire bringing gifts.
In the desert of southern Peru, the Nazca people scratched giant animals and lines into the ground, best seen from the sky.
At Olympia, the sculptor Phidias made a giant seated Zeus of ivory and gold. It stood for about eight hundred years before it was lost.
On the Acropolis of Athens, the Parthenon was completed in marble for the goddess Athena, a model of classical beauty ever since.
In the rainforest of Guatemala, the Maya city of Tikal raised temple pyramids high above the trees.
For the ruler Mausolus, a tomb so grand was built at Halicarnassus that every great tomb since has been called a mausoleum.
In southern Jordan, the Nabataeans carved Petra into rose-coloured cliffs, a city of tombs and temples on the caravan routes.
On Rhodes, a giant bronze sun god guarded the harbour. The Colossus stood for only about half a century before an earthquake brought it down.
At Alexandria, the great lighthouse of Pharos guided ships into harbour for well over a thousand years.
China's first emperor was buried with thousands of life-size clay soldiers, each with its own face, found by farmers in 1974.
In India, monks began cutting the Ajanta Caves into a cliff, filling some thirty Buddhist halls with paintings and sculpture.
Near today's Mexico City rose Teotihuacan, with the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon along a great avenue. Even its builders' name is lost.
In Rome, the Colosseum opened, a vast oval arena where crowds watched gladiators fight. Much of it still stands.
Under Hadrian, Rome rebuilt the Pantheon, its concrete dome open to the sky, the largest of its kind for centuries.
In the Yucatan, the Maya built Chichen Itza, with the stepped pyramid of El Castillo and a great ball court.
In Constantinople, Emperor Justinian raised Hagia Sophia, a church under a soaring dome, later a mosque, a museum, and a mosque again.
In Jerusalem, a golden dome was raised on the Temple Mount, one of the oldest surviving works of Islamic architecture.
On Java, Borobudur was built as a stepped Buddhist mountain of carved reliefs, then lost under ash and jungle for centuries.
Off the coast of Normandy, monks built an abbey on a rocky island that the tide cuts off twice a day: Mont-Saint-Michel.
In London, William the Conqueror began the Tower, palace, prison and treasury, which still guards the Crown Jewels.
In southern Africa, the ancestors of the Shona built the stone walls of Great Zimbabwe, a city of gold and cattle that gave a country its name.
In Cambodia, the Khmer built Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world, now on the country's flag.
In Paris, work began on Notre-Dame, a Gothic cathedral on the Seine that survived a great fire in 2019 and reopened five years later.
In Ethiopia, eleven churches were cut downward into solid rock at Lalibela, where pilgrims still gather today.
Above Granada, the Nasrid kings built the Alhambra, a palace of courtyards, fountains and carved plaster, the jewel of Islamic Spain.
Far out in the Pacific, the Rapa Nui people carved nearly a thousand giant stone figures, the moai of Easter Island. How they moved them is still debated.
In Pisa, a bell tower began to lean on soft ground before it was even finished. It still leans, but engineers have kept it standing.
In Beijing, the Ming emperors built the Forbidden City, a palace of hundreds of buildings, home to emperors for almost five centuries.
High in the Andes, the Inca built Machu Picchu, terraces and temples on a mountain ridge, left empty after the Spanish came.
In Rome, work began on a new St Peter's Basilica. Bramante, Michelangelo and Bernini all shaped it, and Michelangelo's dome crowns the city.
In Moscow, Ivan the Terrible built Saint Basil's Cathedral on Red Square, a cluster of bright onion domes.
In Japan, Himeji Castle was completed, its white walls earning it the name White Heron. It has survived wars, fires and earthquakes.
At Agra, the emperor Shah Jahan finished a white marble tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal: the Taj Mahal.
Outside Paris, Louis the Fourteenth moved his court to Versailles, with its Hall of Mirrors and gardens that palaces across Europe copied.
On a hill in Lhasa, the Potala Palace was completed for the Dalai Lamas, a fortress of white and red over Tibet.
In London, the great clock tower of Parliament was finished, with its bell, Big Ben.
In the Bavarian Alps, King Ludwig the Second built Neuschwanstein, a fairy-tale castle that inspired Disney.
In Barcelona, work began on Gaudi's Sagrada Familia. Well over a century later it is still being built.
In New York harbour, France's gift was unveiled: the Statue of Liberty, her torch greeting millions of arriving immigrants.
For the World's Fair in Paris, the Eiffel Tower rose in wrought iron, the tallest structure on Earth for forty years.
In Mali, the Great Mosque of Djenne was rebuilt in mud brick. Every year the whole town gathers to replaster its walls.
Across Panama, a canal finally joined the Atlantic and the Pacific, lifting ships over the hills in locks, at a heavy cost in lives.
In Manhattan, the Empire State Building went up in just over a year, the tallest building in the world for nearly forty years.
The same year, above Rio de Janeiro, Christ the Redeemer opened his arms over the city from the top of Corcovado.
At the mouth of San Francisco Bay, the Golden Gate Bridge opened, painted international orange, with the longest span of its day.
In South Dakota, four presidents were carved into Mount Rushmore, in the Black Hills that the Lakota hold sacred.
On Sydney Harbour, the Opera House opened under its white sails, designed by Jorn Utzon, who had left before it was done.
And in Dubai, the Burj Khalifa, more than eight hundred metres of glass and steel, the tallest building in the world.
From buried pillars to towers in the clouds, people have never stopped building wonders.
